title: Extreme brainstorming questions: stretch one dimension of your business to nonsense to find 10x ideas
summary: Jason Cohen offers a set of "extreme" hypotheticals (10x prices, no customers, no website, no tech support, one thing this year) that jolt you out of incremental thinking. Each forces a rethink of pricing, positioning, onboarding, growth, and strategy, and sometimes one extreme becomes a company's whole moat.

principles.text: Stretch one dimension to an absurd extreme; a 60% solution there can be a 10x idea in reality.
principles.quote: An idea that would be a 60% solution in an extreme hypothetical case, could be a 2x or even a 10x idea in reality.

principles.text: Unique business models come from being extreme on a dimension competitors and critics consider impossible.
principles.quote: Unique business models emerge when at least one dimension is so extreme that it defies critics and competitors to even conceive of its possibility.

principles.text: Startups undercharge and incumbents fear raising prices; ask what would justify 10x and you can likely justify 2x.
principles.quote: Often early startups charge too little, and established companies struggle to charge more to existing customers.

principles.text: Don't win on features alone; copycats will match them, so differentiate emotionally through brand, trust, and mission.
principles.quote: All your good ideas will be copied; it's just a question of when. Competing only on features results in bullet-point battles; this is the weakest way to win sales.

principles.text: Make the product itself a growth channel; advocates already use it, so build marketing into the product.
principles.quote: Your advocates are already using your product, yet so often we leave "getting more customers" to the marketing department, rather than realizing the product is already a platform for growth.

principles.text: Ask what single initiative you'd ship if you could only ship one thing this year; a business trajectory is usually 1-2 big decisions per year.
principles.quote: When you look back over years of a business, often the whole trajectory comes down to 1-2 big decisions per year.
